newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: FOCUS-Big orders boost Portuguese builders' profit.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Big orders boost Portuguese builders' profit.

text.p: Portuguese construction firms are set to raise profits sharply this year thanks to big order books, dominated by public works projects such as the Lisbon Expo 1998 World Fair, analysts said on Tuesday.

They said building firms would seek to expand operations abroad, via joint ventures, and some could merge or acquire other companies, in order to boost earnings in the medium term as domestic demand was expected to slow down in 1999.
"Construction firms' profits will rise very much this year. They have big order books, including Expo '98 and road building projects," said Joao Pereira of Lisbon-based Espirito Santo Research (ESR).

He forecast that Engil would boost profit to 1.8 billion escudos in 1997 and 2.0 billion in 1998 from 1.5 billion in 1996; Mota & Companhia would raise profit to 2.15 billion escudos in 1997 and 2.6 billion in 1998 from 1.1 billion in 1996; and Somague would hike profit to 1.85 billion in 1997 and 2.1 billion in 1998 from 1.0 billion in 1996.

A London-based analyst, who asked not to be identified, forecast that Engil would boost profit to 1.85 billion escudos in 1997 and 2.17 billion in 1998; Somague would raise profit to 1.8 billion in 1997 and 1.9 billion in 1998; and that Soares da Costa would increase its profit to 1.5 billion in 1997 and 2.3 billion in 1998 from 0.3 billion in 1996.
Mota and Somague shares hit highs of 3,279 escudos and 2,212 escudos respectively on Lisbon bourse on Monday amid optimism that they would post strong results this year, dealers said.
Pereira said Portuguese construction firms, small by international standards, ought to consider merging in line with the trend elsewhere in Europe to raise their capacity to finance big projects.
But the dominance of families in the share ownership of these companies made them less willing to merge.
"These families are used to running their own show. For them, it's their life's work," said Pedro Fonseca of UBS in London.
He said it only made sense for construction firms to merge if they found a partner whose business complemented their own.

Analysts said rumours had circulated in financial markets for months that a Spanish construction company or unlisted Portuguese builder Teixeira Duarte might bid for Soares da Costa, Portugal's biggest builder.
They said Portuguese builder Somague was unlikely to seek any merger or acquisition soon as it was still digesting Assiconstroi, the building subsidiary of A.Silva & Silva that it bought in March.
Pereira said Portuguese builders would seek to participate in joint ventures with Portuguese and foreign companies at home and abroad.
Portuguese construction companies could boost activities in other Portuguese-speaking countries such as Brazil, where they now had a low presence, Angola and Mozambique, analysts said.
Juan Simon of Banco Efisa said Engil and Somague were the most promising Portuguese construction stocks.

He said Engil had low gearing and was involved in the growth area of road building, while Somague was active in project finance projects, including the second bridge over the River Tagus, near Lisbon.
